info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 8.2: Deterministic NLP Tagging, Lemmatization, and Universal Dependencies.

name.text: 01 Question: From Hand Parsing to Algorithmic Pipelines

questiontext.text: Why must digital textual scholars evaluate automated NLP pipelines against an authoritatively verified manual ground truth?

generalfeedback.text: Automated NLP pipelines process large corpora quickly, but their accuracy must be measured against an authoritative manual ground truth.

answer.text: Because automated tools are trained on modern data and often make predictable errors on historical prose.

feedback.text: Correct. Pre-trained models reflect modern language patterns and must be benchmarked against manual historical truth.

answer.text: Because automated tools always produce zero percent accuracy on all text files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern tools often achieve high accuracy, but error rates spike on historical orthography.

answer.text: Because university accreditation rules forbid computers from processing historical manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital humanities encourages automated methods when rigorously validated.

answer.text: Because manual parsing deletes all files from the server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual parsing provides the reference benchmark for testing.

name.text: 02 Question: How Rule-Based Lemmatizers Work

questiontext.text: How does a traditional rule-based lemmatizer determine the dictionary headword for an inflected word?

generalfeedback.text: Rule-based lemmatizers combine suffix-stripping rules with lookup tables of irregular forms to identify base words.

answer.text: By combining suffix-stripping rules with lookup tables of known roots and irregular word forms.

feedback.text: Correct. Rule-based systems strip standard endings (like -ies to -y) and check irregular tables (like went to go).

answer.text: By asking human editors questions over a phone network.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule-based algorithms execute deterministic local code.

answer.text: By translating the word into binary code and measuring electrical resistance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lemmatization is a symbolic and lexicographical algorithm.

answer.text: By picking a random word from the first page of a dictionary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rules follow systematic linguistic algorithms.

name.text: 03 Question: Statistical Sequence Taggers: Parts of Speech in Context

questiontext.text: How do statistical sequence taggers resolve the part of speech for ambiguous homographs like will or est?

generalfeedback.text: Statistical taggers calculate probabilities from surrounding sentence context to predict parts of speech for ambiguous words.

answer.text: By calculating transition probabilities from surrounding words in a sentence based on training corpora.

feedback.text: Correct. Sequence models evaluate neighboring words (such as preceding determiners) to predict the most likely part of speech.

answer.text: By selecting whichever part of speech has the shortest English definition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Statistical taggers evaluate surrounding sentence probabilities, not definition lengths.

answer.text: By refusing to tag any word that appears more than once in a paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Frequent words are processed on every occurrence in context.

answer.text: By converting the entire text into uppercase letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Case conversion does not resolve part-of-speech probabilities.

name.text: 04 Question: TreeTagger: The Probabilistic Decision-Tree Engine

questiontext.text: What algorithmic architecture enables Helmut Schmid's TreeTagger to assign parts of speech and lemmas efficiently?

generalfeedback.text: TreeTagger uses decision trees to assign parts of speech and lemmas rapidly across many historical and modern languages.

answer.text: A decision tree that evaluates sequences of categorical questions about neighboring words.

feedback.text: Correct. TreeTagger uses decision trees to estimate transition probabilities from context.

answer.text: A physical mechanical typewriter installed in a library basement.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TreeTagger is a software application developed in computational linguistics.

answer.text: A search engine crawler that queries public websites in real time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TreeTagger runs locally using pre-compiled parameter files.

answer.text: A random number generator with no linguistic training data.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TreeTagger is trained on curated corpora.

name.text: 05 Question: SpaCy and Stanza: Modern Industrial NLP in Python

questiontext.text: What capability distinguishes modern Python NLP libraries like SpaCy and Stanza?

generalfeedback.text: Python libraries like SpaCy provide fast pre-trained language pipelines that tokenize, tag, lemmatize, and parse sentences with simple code.

answer.text: They provide pre-trained modular pipelines that tokenize, tag parts of speech, lemmatize, and parse syntax with simple code.

feedback.text: Correct. Libraries like SpaCy package tokenizers, taggers, lemmatizers, and parsers into unified Python pipelines.

answer.text: They physically repair torn parchment in library archives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SpaCy is a computational text-processing library.

answer.text: They automatically delete all XML files that contain spelling errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python libraries process text in memory without deleting source files.

answer.text: They require users to write all code in machine binary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SpaCy provides high-level, human-readable Python functions.

name.text: 06 Question: Setting Up Python for Language Processing in VS Code

questiontext.text: What standard Python object in SpaCy holds the processed tokens, lemmas, and syntactic tags for an analyzed sentence?

generalfeedback.text: A short Python script using SpaCy can load a pre-trained model and print lemmas, parts of speech, and syntactic relations in seconds.

answer.text: A Doc container object iterated over individual Token objects.

feedback.text: Correct. Passing text to a SpaCy model returns a Doc object containing Token instances with attributes like lemma_ and pos_.

answer.text: An unformatted plain-text bitmap image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SpaCy returns structured linguistic Python objects.

answer.text: A locked PDF file stored in the trash.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Doc object is an active in-memory data structure.

answer.text: A hardware serial port address.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Token attributes are accessed via standard Python object properties.

name.text: 07 Question: The Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) Dilemma

questiontext.text: What causes the Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) problem when running modern NLP pipelines on historical documents?

generalfeedback.text: The Out-of-Vocabulary problem occurs when historical words or unusual spellings are missing from an automated model's training dictionary.

answer.text: Historical words or archaic spellings do not exist in the modern dictionary data used to train the software.

feedback.text: Correct. Models trained on modern texts lack entries for eighteenth-century orthography and scribal variants.

answer.text: The computer hard drive runs completely out of digital storage space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. OOV refers to missing lexical items in a language model, not disk space.

answer.text: The text file is encrypted with military-grade passwords.

feedback.text: Incorrect. OOV occurs on readable, unencrypted historical text.

answer.text: The software refuses to parse words containing more than three vowels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Word length does not trigger OOV failures; absent lexicon entries do.

name.text: 08 Question: Handling Historical Orthography in Deterministic Models

questiontext.text: Why do eighteenth-century French spellings like décrétoit or English spellings like shew'd trigger errors in modern taggers?

generalfeedback.text: Historical spelling variations like French -oit or English shew'd confuse automated taggers because they deviate from modern training lexica.

answer.text: Modern training lexica expect standardized forms like décrétait and showed, failing to recognize archaic suffixes.

feedback.text: Correct. Deviations from modern standardized orthography prevent models from matching words in their internal lexica.

answer.text: Historical scribes wrote in secret mathematical ciphers designed to prevent reading.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Premodern archival records were written for contemporary human comprehension.

answer.text: Eighteenth-century words contain characters that cannot be rendered in Unicode.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical alphabetic text is fully encoded in UTF-8.

answer.text: Modern software automatically deletes any word older than fifty years.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software processes text without temporal deletion rules.

name.text: 09 Question: Universal Dependencies in Automated NLP

questiontext.text: Why is it beneficial that tools like SpaCy and Stanza output standard Universal Dependencies tags by default?

generalfeedback.text: Modern NLP libraries output Universal Dependencies tags by default, allowing direct side-by-side comparison with your manual ground truth.

answer.text: Their predictions can be directly compared against your manual ground truth without translating between naming systems.

feedback.text: Correct. Shared UPOS and FEATS standards allow immediate side-by-side automated evaluation.

answer.text: It forces all languages to translate their text into French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Universal Dependencies provides grammatical labels, not translation.

answer.text: It prevents students from seeing any errors made by the computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standardized tags make errors immediately apparent in comparative audits.

answer.text: It changes the historical author's name in the teiHeader.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linguistic tagging does not alter metadata author credits.

name.text: 10 Question: Tokenization Pitfalls in French: Clitics and Apostrophes

questiontext.text: What common tokenization error occurs when automated taggers process French phrases with apostrophes (like l'assemblée)?

generalfeedback.text: In French text, verify that automated tokenizers split apostrophe clitics cleanly so that articles and nouns receive separate tags.

answer.text: Failing to split the clitic article from the noun, causing the entire string to be misclassified as a single unit.

feedback.text: Correct. Keeping l'assemblée as one token prevents both the determiner and the noun from receiving clean tags.

answer.text: Deleting the noun and keeping only the letter L.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tokenizers do not delete words; they split or merge characters.

answer.text: Replacing the apostrophe with an exclamation mark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation is preserved or separated, not swapped for other marks.

answer.text: Translating the French noun into German.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tokenization segments text in its original language.

name.text: 11 Question: Tokenization Pitfalls in English: Contractions and Hyphens

questiontext.text: How do modern English tokenizers typically handle informal contractions like can't or didn't?

generalfeedback.text: Verify how automated tokenizers handle informal contractions and historical compound adverbs against your project policies.

answer.text: They split the contraction into two syntactic tokens, separating the auxiliary verb from the negative particle.

feedback.text: Correct. Splitting can't into ca + n't allows the helping verb and negative adverb to be tagged independently.

answer.text: They delete the contraction and insert a question mark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation and letters are preserved across tokens.

answer.text: They merge the entire paragraph into one giant compound word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tokenizers segment sentences into individual word units.

answer.text: They convert negative contractions into positive verbs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Grammatical tokenization preserves semantic polarity.

name.text: 12 Question: Homograph Disambiguation Under the Microscope

questiontext.text: In the sentence The Chief will observe this Treaty of his own free will, how does a statistical model determine that the second will is a noun?

generalfeedback.text: Statistical models use neighboring words to disambiguate homographs, succeeding on standard syntax but stumbling on unusual historical phrasing.

answer.text: It evaluates preceding words like own free, recognizing that adjectives typically modify nouns.

feedback.text: Correct. Neighboring adjective modifiers provide strong statistical evidence that will functions as a noun.

answer.text: It consults an astrological horoscope to make its choice.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models rely on mathematical transition probabilities from surrounding text.

answer.text: It assumes the first occurrence of any word is a verb and all subsequent occurrences are nouns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tagging evaluates local syntactic context, not arbitrary position rules.

answer.text: It deletes the second word because repetitions are prohibited.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Repetitions are tagged based on their immediate syntactic environment.

name.text: 13 Question: Universal Dependencies Syntactic Relations (DEPREL)

questiontext.text: Which Universal Dependencies relation tag labels the nominal subject of an active transitive verb?

generalfeedback.text: Dependency relation tags like nsubj, obj, and case describe the specific grammatical jobs that words perform in clauses.

answer.text: nsubj

feedback.text: Correct. nsubj identifies the nominal subject governing an active verb predicate.

answer.text: obj

feedback.text: Incorrect. obj identifies the direct object receiving the action.

answer.text: amod

feedback.text: Incorrect. amod identifies an adjectival modifier.

answer.text: punct

feedback.text: Incorrect. punct identifies punctuation marks.

name.text: 14 Question: Heads and Dependents in Automated Trees

questiontext.text: What role does the main finite verb serve in a dependency grammar sentence tree?

generalfeedback.text: Dependency parsers link every word to a governing head word, creating a rooted tree centered on the main finite verb.

answer.text: The structural root of the sentence, possessing no governing head within the clause.

feedback.text: Correct. The main verb serves as the root (Head = 0) from which all subjects, objects, and modifiers depend.

answer.text: A minor dependent modifier attached to a punctuation mark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation attaches to the clause, while the verb governs the sentence.

answer.text: The direct object of the first preposition in the sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prepositions govern nouns; the main finite verb serves as the clause root.

answer.text: An external metadata tag stored only in the teiHeader.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verbs are syntactic words in the running text body.

name.text: 15 Question: Visualizing Dependency Trees with displaCy

questiontext.text: What visual insight does the displaCy rendering tool provide to an editor?

generalfeedback.text: Visualizing syntax trees with displaCy turns abstract dependency relations into clear graphical diagrams of sentence structure.

answer.text: It renders sentence syntax as an interactive graphical diagram with directed arrows linking heads to dependents.

feedback.text: Correct. displaCy draws visual arcs between words labeled with their dependency relation tags.

answer.text: It generates three-dimensional animated cartoons of manuscript authors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. displaCy renders linguistic dependency trees, not character animations.

answer.text: It displays a satellite map showing where the parchment was manufactured.

feedback.text: Incorrect. displaCy visualizes grammatical syntax.

answer.text: It hides all text and shows only black rectangles on screen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. displaCy makes sentence structure transparent and legible.

questiontext.text: How do Python NLP scripts format automated linguistic annotations for export to CoNLL-U files?

generalfeedback.text: On formal clauses with standard grammar, modern automated pipelines can achieve high accuracy matching human ground truth.

answer.text: Because the vocabulary is formal and standard, and the passive syntax matches patterns in modern training data.

feedback.text: Correct. Standard spelling and clear syntax allow modern statistical models to predict tags accurately.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Treaty was composed in the eighteenth century by colonial officials.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All words were evaluated in running sequence.

name.text: 18 Question: Running an NLP Pipeline on the 1791 French Decree

questiontext.text: Under what condition does an automated French model begin to fail on an eighteenth-century decree?

generalfeedback.text: French pre-trained models handle standard vocabulary accurately, but require normalized spelling to parse older texts correctly.

answer.text: When it encounters eighteenth-century verbal spellings (like décrétoit) that deviate from modern training lexica.

feedback.text: Correct. Archaic spelling variants trigger Out-of-Vocabulary errors and misclassified parts of speech.

answer.text: When the decree mentions the National Assembly.

answer.text: When the document is written on handmade rag paper.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical paper composition does not affect digital text algorithms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern pipelines routinely process long texts.

questiontext.text: In Maud Lewis's sentence I received your letter today, what caused the disagreement between SpaCy and our manual ground truth on your?

feedback.text: Correct. Editorial policy in our ground truth mapped your to lemma you, whereas SpaCy cited your as its own headword.

answer.text: SpaCy concluded that Maud Lewis was writing in sixteenth-century Latin.

answer.text: SpaCy deleted the word your because it was misspelled.

questiontext.text: How is token-level part-of-speech accuracy calculated in computational textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: Calculate separate accuracy scores for parts of speech and lemmas by comparing automated output directly to your manual ground truth.

answer.text: By dividing the number of correctly tagged tokens by the total number of tokens evaluated and multiplying by 100.

answer.text: By multiplying the word count by the price of the software.

name.text: 23 Question: Diagnosing Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) Failures

questiontext.text: What is the identity fallback symptom in an Out-of-Vocabulary lemmatization failure?

generalfeedback.text: OOV failures typically show up as copied surface spellings, invented headwords, or default noun tags.

answer.text: The model copies the inflected surface spelling directly into the lemma field because it cannot find the root.

feedback.text: Correct. When a model cannot find a headword, it frequently falls back to outputting the surface token as the lemma.

answer.text: The model replaces the user's name on their university ID card.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Identity fallback refers to duplicating surface strings into lemma fields.

answer.text: The model converts all text into French automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fallback copies the source token verbatim.

answer.text: The computer reboots into safe mode.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Identity fallback is an algorithm output behavior, not a system crash.

questiontext.text: Why does an eighteenth-century English verb form like witnesseth often deceive modern automated taggers?

generalfeedback.text: Historical inflectional endings like French -oit or English -eth trigger errors because modern statistical models do not recognize them as active verb suffixes.

answer.text: Because the archaic -eth suffix is absent from active modern verb paradigms, leading models to guess noun or adjective.

feedback.text: Correct. Modern language models are trained on contemporary endings and misclassify obsolete inflectional suffixes.

answer.text: Because words ending in -th are prohibited in English legal documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Formal legal instruments made extensive use of archaic suffixes.

answer.text: Because the word contains too many syllables to fit into computer memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Memory buffers easily handle polysyllabic words.

answer.text: Because the scribe wrote the word using invisible ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical ink is fully visible on the parchment leaf.
